source_text: Jungat epistola, quos jungit sacerdotium : immo charta non dividat, quos Christi nectit amor. Commentarios in Osee, Amos, Zachariam, Malachiam, quos poscitis, scripsissem, si licuisset præ valitudine. Mittitis solatia sumptuum : notarios nostros et librarios sustentatis, ut vobis potissimum nostrum sudet ingenium. Et ecce ex latere frequens turba diversa poscentium, quasi aut æquum sit, me vobis esurientibus, aliis laborare : aut in ratione dati et accepti, cuiquam, præter vobis, obnoxius sim. Itaque longa ægrotatione fractus, ne penitus hoc anno reticerem, et apud vos mutus essem, tridui opus vestro nomini consecravi, interpretationem videlicet trium Salomonis voluminum, משלי, quas Hebræi Parabolas, vulgata editio Proverbia vocat, קוהלת, qui Græce Ecclesiasten, Latine Concionatorem possumus dicere, שיר השירים, quod in nostram linguam vertitur Canticum canticorum. Fertur et Panæretos Iesu filii Sirach liber, et alius pseudepigraphus, qui Sapientia Salomonis inscribitur. Quorum priorem Hebraicum reperi : non Ecclesiasticum, ut apud Latinos, sed Parabolas prænotatum, cui juncti erant Ecclesiastes et Canticum canticorum : ut similitudinem Salomonis, non solum librorum numero, sed etiam materiarum genere coæquaret. Secundus apud Hebræos nusquam est, quin et ipse stylus, Græcam eloquentiam redolet : et nonnulli scriptorum veterum hunc esse Judæi Philonis affirmant. Sicut ergo Judith, et Tobiæ, et Machabæorum libros legit quidem Ecclesia, sed inter canonicas scripturas non recipit : sic et hæc duo volumina legat ad ædificationem plebis, non ad auctoritatem Ecclesiasticorum dogmatum confirmandam. Si cui sane Septuaginta interpretum magis editio placet, habet eam a nobis olim emendatam. Neque enim nova sic cudimus, ut vetera destruamus. Et tamen cum diligentissime legerit, sciat magis nostra intellegi, quæ non in tertium vas transfusa coacuerint, sed statim de prælo purissimæ commendata testæ, suum saporem servaverint.
thought_title: Jerome dedicates his three-day translation of Solomon's three books to Paula and Eustochium
orientation: Jerome is writing to Paula and Eustochium, dedicating to them his translation of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs, and explaining the canonical status of Wisdom and Sirach.
pass_a_gloss: Let the letter join those whom the priesthood joins; rather, let not paper divide those whom the love of Christ binds. I would have written the commentaries on Hosea, Amos, Zechariah, Malachi, which you request, if it had been permitted on account of ill health. You send the comfort of funds; you support our secretaries and copyists, so that our talent may sweat especially for you. And behold, from the side there is a frequent crowd of various people making requests, as if either it were fair that I labor for others while you are hungry, or that in the account of giving and receiving I be bound to anyone besides you. Therefore, broken by long illness, lest I be completely silent this year and be mute among you, I have consecrated to your name the work of three days, namely the translation of the three volumes of Solomon: Proverbs, which the Hebrews call Parables, the common edition calls Proverbs; Ecclesiastes, which in Greek we can call Ecclesiastes, in Latin the Preacher; Song of Songs, which is translated into our language as Song of Songs. There is also circulated the book of Panaretos of Jesus son of Sirach, and another falsely attributed book, which is inscribed the Wisdom of Solomon. Of these, I found the former in Hebrew: not Ecclesiasticus, as among the Latins, but entitled Parables, to which were joined Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs, so that it might equal the likeness of Solomon not only in the number of books but also in the kind of subject matter. The second is nowhere among the Hebrews, and indeed the very style reeks of Greek eloquence; and some of the ancient writers affirm that this is the work of Philo the Jew. Therefore, just as the Church indeed reads the books of Judith and Tobit and Maccabees, but does not receive them among the canonical scriptures, so also let it read these two volumes for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines. If indeed the edition of the Septuagint pleases anyone more, he has it, emended by us long ago. For we do not forge new things in such a way that we destroy old things. And yet, when he has read very diligently, let him know that our things are understood more, which have not turned sour by being poured into a third vessel, but, immediately entrusted from the wine-press to the purest earthenware, have kept their own flavor.

choices.why: The Greek title is kept as a proper name, matching the source form and the brief's name map.
The glossary requires this rendering for the term.
The Latin title is kept as a proper name, contrasting with the Hebrew title Parables.
The glossary requires 'canon' for canon-related terms; 'canonical scriptures' preserves the adjective form.
The metaphor is of wine or oil pressing, not printing; the source uses the image of fresh wine from the press.
The image is of wine stored in a clean clay vessel, preserving its flavor.

pass_b_english: Let a letter join those whom the priesthood joins; indeed, let not paper divide those whom the love of Christ binds. I would have written the commentaries on Hosea, Amos, Zechariah, and Malachi that you request, if my health had permitted it. You send me the support of funds; you sustain my secretaries and copyists, so that my talent may labor especially for you. And look—from every side a crowd of people with different demands presses in, as if it were fair for me to work for others while you go hungry, or as if in the account of giving and receiving I were obligated to anyone besides you. And so, broken by a long illness, so that I would not be entirely silent this year and mute before you, I have consecrated to your name a work of three days—namely, a translation of three volumes of Solomon: Proverbs, which the Hebrews call Parables and the common edition calls Proverbs; Ecclesiastes, which in Greek we can call Ecclesiastes and in Latin the Preacher; and Song of Songs, which is rendered into our language as the Song of Songs. There is also circulated the book of Panaretos, Jesus son of Sirach, and another falsely attributed book, which is inscribed as the Wisdom of Solomon. The former I found in Hebrew, not titled Ecclesiasticus as among the Latins, but Parables, joined with Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, so that it might match the likeness of Solomon not only in the number of books but also in the kind of their subjects. The second is nowhere among the Hebrews, and indeed its very style reeks of Greek eloquence; and some of the ancient writers affirm that this is the work of Philo the Jew. Therefore, just as the Church reads the books of Judith, Tobit, and the Maccabees but does not receive them among the canonical scriptures, so also it may read these two volumes for the edification of the people, but not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines. If indeed anyone prefers the edition of the Septuagint, he has it, emended by me long ago. For we do not forge new things in such a way as to destroy the old. And yet, when he has read very carefully, let him know that our translation is better understood, because it has not turned sour by being poured into a third vessel, but has preserved its own flavor, having been entrusted immediately from the wine-press to the purest earthenware.

last_rejected.quote: Ecclesiastes, which in Greek we can call Ecclesiastes and in Latin the Preacher
last_rejected.source_quote: קוהלת, qui Græce Ecclesiasten, Latine Concionatorem possumus dicere
last_rejected.why: Source says 'which we can call Ecclesiastes in Greek, the Preacher in Latin'; English redundantly repeats Ecclesiastes for Greek.
last_rejected.fix: Ecclesiastes, which we can call Ecclesiastes in Greek and the Preacher in Latin
last_rejected.ruling: English accurately renders 'qui Græce Ecclesiasten, Latine Concionatorem possumus dicere'—'which in Greek we can call Ecclesiastes and in Latin the Preacher.' The claim misreads: source says 'Ecclesiasten' (Greek form), not 'Ecclesiastes' (Latin title). English correctly distinguishes Greek 'Ecclesiasten' from Latin title usage, matching source structure.

last_rejected.quote: not titled Ecclesiasticus as among the Latins, but Parables
last_rejected.source_quote: non Ecclesiasticum, ut apud Latinos, sed Parabolas prænotatum
last_rejected.why: Latin 'Ecclesiasticum' refers to the book's title, not 'Ecclesiasticus'; Jerome says it's 'not titled Ecclesiasticum among Latins but marked as Parables'
last_rejected.fix: not titled Ecclesiasticum as among the Latins, but marked as Parables
last_rejected.ruling: 'Ecclesiasticum' is neuter accusative agreeing with 'librum' (the book Ecclesiasticus); 'titled Ecclesiasticus' correctly renders the book title.

last_rejected.why: 'similitudinem' means 'likeness' in sense of 'image/portrait', but here means 'similarity' or 'parallel'—the collection matches Solomon's threefold output
last_rejected.ruling: 'similitudo' here means 'likeness/similarity'; 'match the likeness of Solomon' adequately conveys the parallel in number and subject matter.

last_rejected.quote: so also it may read these two volumes
last_rejected.source_quote: sic et hæc duo volumina legat
last_rejected.why: legat is jussive: Jerome tells the Church to read them, not merely that it may.
last_rejected.fix: so also let it read these two volumes for the edification of the people, not to confirm the authority of church doctrines.
last_rejected.ruling: "legat" is a present subjunctive; "it may read" is a standard rendering of jussive/permissive sense, parallel to "legit... non recipit". Meaning is essentially preserved.

last_rejected.quote: the book of Panaretos, Jesus son of Sirach
last_rejected.why: Panaretos is the book’s title; Jesus son of Sirach is the author, not another name for Panaretos.
last_rejected.fix: There also circulates the book Panaretos, by Jesus son of Sirach.
last_rejected.ruling: "Panæretos Iesu filii Sirach liber" is Panaretos (all-virtuous, an epithet of the book) with the author in the genitive; the English reads acceptably as an appositional title and author.
